questions.q: Kavya sets her compass to 4 cm against a ruler, fixes the pointed tip at P and starts turning. Halfway round, the legs slip open a little, to about 4.4 cm, and she carries on to complete the turn. Which statement about the finished curve is correct?
questions.a: It is not a circle, because the points drawn after the slip are farther from P than the points drawn before it
o: It is not a circle, because the points drawn after the slip are farther from P than the points drawn before it
It is a circle of radius 4.4 cm, because the last setting is the one that decides the radius
It is a circle of radius 4 cm, because the tip never left P
It is two half circles with the same centre, so it is a circle with two radii

questions.q: For a decorative wave, Dhruv draws a half circle on a stretch AX of the central line, putting the compass tip at the middle of AX so that the half circle ends exactly at A and at X. His compass is set to 2.5 cm. How long is the stretch AX?
questions.a: 5 cm
o: 5 cm
2.5 cm, because the radius and the stretch must be equal
7.5 cm, because the stretch is taken as three times the radius
1.25 cm, because the radius is half the stretch

questions.q: A compass is set to 4 cm and its tip is placed at P. After the circle is drawn, Mira lays a ruler from P to a point Z on the curve and reads 3.8 cm. Which explanation fits this reading best?
questions.a: The tip slipped from P or the opening changed while drawing, since every point of a correct circle is 4 cm from P
o: The tip slipped from P or the opening changed while drawing, since every point of a correct circle is 4 cm from P
The reading is right, because points on a circle are at different distances from the centre in different directions
The reading is right, because Z lies on the curve and a curve is always shorter than the setting
The compass was set against the ruler wrongly, but Z is still a correct point of the circle

questions.q: A circle is drawn with centre P. On it a point A is found to be 5 cm from P. Rohit marks another point B on the same circle, in a completely different direction. What can he say about PB without measuring?
questions.a: PB is also 5 cm, because both points lie on the circle drawn around P
o: PB is also 5 cm, because both points lie on the circle drawn around P
PB is shorter than 5 cm if B lies below the line PA
PB can be anything from 0 to 10 cm, since B is in a different direction
PB must be 10 cm if B is opposite to A, because the two radii join up

questions.q: Asha marks the points 4 cm east, west, north and south of P with a ruler and says, 'These are all the points 4 cm from P.' Which reply is correct?
questions.a: No; points in every other direction are also 4 cm from P, and together they form a circle
o: No; points in every other direction are also 4 cm from P, and together they form a circle
Yes; the four directions are the only ones in which a distance can be measured exactly
Yes; any other point at 4 cm from P would have to be on the same four lines
No; only the east and west points are at 4 cm, the others are nearer to P

questions.q:
Anita is told to draw a circle of radius 6 cm.
Statement 1: She opens the compass until the tip and the pencil are 6 cm apart on the ruler.
Statement 2: She keeps the pencil end of the compass fixed and moves the pointed tip round it.
Statement 3: Every point on her finished curve is 6 cm from the point where the tip was placed.
Which of these are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
all three

questions.q:
Assertion (A): When a circle of radius 4 cm is drawn around P with a compass, every point on it measures 4 cm from P.
Reason (R): The pointed tip stays fixed at P and the distance between the tip and the pencil does not change while the pencil moves.
questions.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: Neha sets her compass to 2 cm and draws wavy-line half circles end to end, each with the tip at the middle of its stretch and ending at both ends of the stretch. The number of such half circles that cover a central line of 24 cm exactly is ___.

A compass is opened to 4 cm and the tip is placed at P. (a) Rohit lays a ruler from P to any point on the curve. What reading should he get? (b) He finds one point reading 4.6 cm. Give two things that may have gone wrong while drawing.
questions.a: (a) 4 cm, for every point on the curve. (b) The tip may have slipped from P, or the opening may have changed (legs slid open) during the turn; either makes some points farther than 4 cm.
s: Part (a): 4 cm for every point
Part (b): gives two causes, the tip slipping and the opening changing

questions.q: Priya draws a round shape freehand around a point P and checks three points on it: they are 3.8 cm, 4.1 cm and 4.0 cm from P. (a) Is her shape a circle of radius 4 cm? (b) What would the three readings be if she had used a compass set to 4 cm?
questions.a: (a) No, because its points are not all the same distance from P; it is only close to a circle. (b) All three readings would be 4 cm.
s: Part (a): No, with the reason that the distances differ
Part (b): all three readings 4 cm

questions.q: Two circles are drawn with the same centre P, one with the compass set to 2 cm and the other set to 3 cm. (a) Which circle lies farther from P? (b) Along a ruler laid from P in any direction, how far apart are the two curves, and why is the gap the same in every direction?
questions.a: (a) The 3 cm circle. (b) 3 - 2 = 1 cm, in every direction, because each curve is at a fixed distance from P in every direction.
s: Part (a): the circle set to 3 cm
Part (b): 1 cm, with the reason that each is a constant distance from P

questions.q: While drawing a circle, why must the pointed tip of the compass stay at one place, and what shape results if the tip is allowed to wander slightly during the turn?
questions.a: The tip is the centre, and all points of a circle must be the same distance from the centre. If it wanders, the distances differ, so the curve is an uneven, wobbly shape and not a circle.
s: Says the tip marks the centre and the distance to it must stay fixed
Says a wandering tip gives an uneven shape that is not a circle

questions.q: True or False: A compass is set to a gap of 5 cm. Whether the tip is placed at P or at Q, the circle drawn has a radius of 5 cm. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. The radius is the distance from the centre to the curve, which is set by the opening of the compass (5 cm); placing the tip elsewhere only moves the circle, it does not change its radius.
s: States True
Reason: the radius depends on the opening, the position of the tip fixes only where the centre is

questions.q: Tara says: 'When I draw a circle of radius 6 cm, only the point where the pencil starts is exactly 6 cm from the centre. The other points are only approximately 6 cm away.' Is she right? Explain using how the compass is used.
questions.a: No. The tip stays at the centre and the opening stays 6 cm for the whole turn, so every point the pencil marks is 6 cm from the centre, not only the starting point. (Small errors come only from a slipped tip or a changed opening.)
s: Verdict: No
Uses the fixed tip and fixed opening
Concludes that all points, not just the first, are 6 cm away, with errors due only to slipping

questions.q: Place Q 4 cm east of P. Zara draws a circle of radius 4 cm with centre P and another of radius 4 cm with centre Q, and says, 'A point that is 4 cm from Q must also be 4 cm from P.' Show with a point of her second circle that this is impossible to conclude.
questions.a: The point 4 cm east of Q is on the circle centred at Q. Its distance from P is 4 + 4 = 8 cm, not 4 cm. So a point on the circle around Q need not be 4 cm from P; it is 4 cm from P only if it is also on the circle around P.
s: Picks a point of the circle centred at Q, such as the one 4 cm east of Q
Finds its distance from P is 8 cm
Concludes that a point 4 cm from Q is not necessarily 4 cm from P

questions.q: A craft club must draw eight badges, each a circle of radius 3.5 cm, on one chart. State what must be kept the same for all eight circles, what must change from one badge to the next, and how they check one badge afterwards.
questions.a: Kept the same: the compass opening of 3.5 cm against the ruler. Changed: the place of the pointed tip, because each badge needs its own centre. Check: measure from the centre to a few points on the curve; each should read 3.5 cm.
s: The opening of 3.5 cm stays the same
The position of the tip (the centre) changes for each badge
Checks by measuring from the centre to points on the curve

questions.q: On a central line AB of 20 cm, Gauri draws half-circle waves end to end. For each wave the compass tip is at the middle of its stretch of the line and the half circle ends at both ends of the stretch. (a) With a compass opening of 2 cm, how long is each stretch? (b) How many waves cover AB exactly? (c) With an opening of 2.5 cm, how many waves cover AB exactly? (d) With an opening of 3 cm, how many whole waves fit and how much of AB is left? (e) Of the three openings 2 cm, 2.5 cm and 3 cm, which covers AB exactly with the fewest waves, and how many times must she place the tip then?
questions.a: (a) 4 cm. (b) 20 / 4 = 5 waves. (c) The stretch is 5 cm, so 20 / 5 = 4 waves. (d) The stretch is 6 cm; 3 whole waves use 18 cm and 2 cm is left. (e) Of those three, the 2.5 cm opening: it covers AB exactly with 4 waves, so the tip is placed 4 times (the 3 cm opening does not cover it exactly).
s: Part (a): 4 cm
Part (b): 5 waves
Part (c): 4 waves
Part (d): 3 waves with 2 cm left
Part (e): opening 2.5 cm and 4 placements, rejecting 3 cm because 2 cm is left over

questions.q: For a target design, concentric circles are drawn around a point P. The first has radius 1.5 cm and each next circle has a radius 1.5 cm larger, up to five circles. (a) List the five radii. (b) What opening is the compass set to for the fourth circle? (c) How far apart are the second and fifth circles along a ruler laid from P? (d) A pin mark is 5.2 cm from P. Between which two circles does it lie? (e) After the first circle, how many times does she change the opening?
questions.a: (a) 1.5, 3, 4.5, 6, 7.5 cm. (b) 6 cm. (c) 7.5 - 3 = 4.5 cm. (d) Between the 4.5 cm and 6 cm circles, since 4.5 < 5.2 < 6. (e) 4 times, once for each of the circles after the first.
s: Part (a): the five radii
Part (b): 6 cm
Part (c): 4.5 cm
Part (d): between 4.5 cm and 6 cm, with the comparison
Part (e): 4 changes of opening

questions.q: A club paints a wavy border along a central line AB of 30 cm. The wave is a row of identical half circles end to end, each drawn with the compass tip at the middle of its own stretch of AB, so a half circle with opening r cm sits on a stretch of 2r cm. The club can set its compass only to whole or half centimetres, wants the half circles to cover AB exactly with no gap left, wants at least 5 and at most 7 waves, and every wave needs one placement of the tip. (a) Find the stretch and the number of waves for an opening of 2 cm and say whether it meets the aim. (b) Find the number of waves for an opening of 2.5 cm. (c) Find the number of waves for an opening of 3 cm. (d) Both of the last two meet the club's aim. Which one would you recommend and why?
questions.a: (a) Stretch 4 cm; 30 / 4 = 7.5, so 7 whole waves leave 2 cm uncovered: it fails the 'exactly' aim. (b) Stretch 5 cm; 30 / 5 = 6 waves. (c) Stretch 6 cm; 30 / 6 = 5 waves. (d) Either is supportable: 2.5 cm gives 6 smaller, finer waves but needs 6 placements of the tip; 3 cm gives 5 larger waves and only 5 placements, with less chance of uneven waves. A reasonable recommendation is 3 cm if time and neatness matter, 2.5 cm if a finer border matters more.
s: Part (a): stretch 4 cm, 7 waves with 2 cm left, so it fails
Part (b): 6 waves
Part (c): 5 waves
Part (d): chooses one and weighs 6 finer waves and 6 placements against 5 larger waves and 5 placements

questions.q: On a school map drawn to the scale 1 cm for 25 m (so a compass opening of 1 cm on the map stands for 25 m on the ground), a compass circle is drawn around an assembly point P. From P, the library is 3.5 cm away on the map, the canteen 4 cm and the lab 4.3 cm. The fire rule says every building must lie within 110 m of the assembly point. A second possible point Q has its farthest building at 4.2 cm on the map, but Q is 40 m from the school gate while P is only 20 m from the gate. (a) What compass opening, in cm, draws the circle through the lab around P, and what real distance is that? (b) Does P meet the 110 m rule? Does Q? (c) Which building lies on the circle drawn with opening 4 cm around P? (d) The principal must pick P or Q. Weigh the margin under the rule against the gate distance and recommend one.
questions.a: (a) 4.3 cm, and 4.3 x 25 = 107.5 m. (b) P: 107.5 m is within 110 m, so P passes. Q: 4.2 x 25 = 105 m, so Q passes. (c) The canteen, since 4 cm is its distance from P; the library (3.5 cm) is inside the circle and the lab (4.3 cm) outside. (d) Both meet the rule, so the choice is a trade-off: Q has a 5 m margin under the rule against 2.5 m for P, but Q is 40 m from the gate against 20 m for P. Either can be defended; a good answer names both numbers, for example choosing P because a 2.5 m margin still satisfies the rule and the gate is 20 m nearer, or Q if the rule is to be kept with more room.
s: Part (a): 4.3 cm and 107.5 m
Part (b): both pass, at 107.5 m and 105 m
Part (c): the canteen is on the circle
Part (d): weighs the margins 2.5 m and 5 m against the gate distances 20 m and 40 m and recommends one

questions.q: A rectangular notice board has corners W, X, Y and Z in order around its frame. A student lists possible names for it. Which one cannot be a name of this board?
questions.a: WXZY
o: WXZY
XYZW
ZYXW
YZWX

questions.q: A square piece of paper has sides of 5 cm and four right angles. It is then turned through an eighth of a turn on the table so that its corners point up, down, left and right. Rohan says, 'It is now a diamond, so it has stopped being a square.' Which reply is correct?
questions.a: It is still a square, because turning leaves every side at 5 cm and every angle at 90 degrees
o: It is still a square, because turning leaves every side at 5 cm and every angle at 90 degrees
It is a square only if it is turned back, because squares must have a horizontal side
It is a rectangle now, because the sides are no longer parallel to the table edge
It is neither, because the corners no longer point where the original corners did

questions.q: A four-sided figure has all four angles equal to 90 degrees, and its sides measure 3 cm, 5 cm, 3 cm and 5 cm in order around it. Which description is correct?
questions.a: It is a rectangle but not a square, because opposite sides are equal and the adjacent sides are not
o: It is a rectangle but not a square, because opposite sides are equal and the adjacent sides are not
It is a square, because all four of its angles are 90 degrees
It is a square, because opposite sides are equal in length
It is neither, because a rectangle needs all four sides equal

questions.q: On a dot grid, corners P, Q, R and S are joined in order. Going from P to Q is 3 dots right and 1 up. From Q to R is 1 left and 3 up. From R to S is 3 left and 1 down. From S back to P is 1 right and 3 down. Without a ruler, which conclusion is justified?
questions.a: PQRS is a square, because every step is the previous one turned through a right angle, so all sides match and all angles are 90 degrees
o: PQRS is a square, because every step is the previous one turned through a right angle, so all sides match and all angles are 90 degrees
PQRS is a rectangle but not a square, because it is drawn tilted on the grid
PQRS is a square only if the sides are measured with a ruler first
PQRS is not a square, because no side runs along a row or column of dots

questions.q: Which of these is NOT true of every rectangle?
questions.a: All four sides are equal
o: All four sides are equal
Opposite sides are equal in length
Every angle is 90 degrees
It is still a rectangle after being rotated

questions.q:
Consider rectangle ABCD and square PQRS.
Statement 1: ADCB is a valid name for rectangle ABCD.
Statement 2: Every rectangle satisfies both S1 (all sides equal) and R2 (all angles 90 degrees).
Statement 3: Turning a rectangle on the table does not change its side lengths or its angles.
Which of these are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only
o: 1 and 3 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
all three

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Rectangle PQRS can also be named SRQP.
Reason (R): Every angle of a rectangle is 90 degrees.
questions.a: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: The corners A, B, C and D can be written in 24 different orders. Of these, the number of orders that are valid names for rectangle ABCD is ___.

Match each figure in Column I with its description in Column II.
Column I: 1. A paper square after a quarter of a turn on the table  2. A figure with four right angles and sides 4 cm, 6 cm, 4 cm, 6 cm  3. The order ACBD for a rectangle ABCD  4. A figure with sides 7 cm, 7 cm, 7 cm, 7 cm and four right angles
Column II: A. A square  B. A rectangle that is not a square  C. Not a valid name  D. Has the same sides and angles as before the turn
Square PQRS has its corners in that order around it. (a) Write two valid names for it other than PQRS. (b) Explain why PRQS is not a valid name.
questions.a: (a) Any two of QRSP, RSPQ, SPQR, SRQP, RQPS, QPSR, PSRQ. (b) In PRQS the second corner R is not next to P: the travel jumps across the figure from P to R, so the corners are not in the order met going around.
s: Part (a): two correct names, e.g. SPQR and PSRQ
Part (b): says PRQS skips a corner so it is not in the order of travel around the figure

questions.q: A rectangle has sides 12 cm and 5 cm. It is turned so that its 12 cm sides become the vertical ones. (a) What are its side lengths and angles now? (b) Is it still a rectangle? Use the properties R1 and R2.
questions.a: (a) Sides still 12, 5, 12, 5 cm and every angle still 90 degrees. (b) Yes: opposite sides are still equal (R1) and all angles are still 90 degrees (R2).
s: Part (a): same lengths and angles, because turning changes neither
Part (b): Yes, with both R1 and R2 checked

questions.q: Name the property that a square has but a general rectangle does not, and give the sides of one rectangle that fails it.
questions.a: A square has all sides equal (S1); a general rectangle has only opposite sides equal. A rectangle with sides 4 cm and 6 cm has all angles 90 degrees but its sides are not all equal.
s: Names S1, all four sides equal
Gives a rectangle such as 4 cm by 6 cm that fails it

questions.q: (a) Can a four-sided figure have all four angles equal to 90 degrees and yet have opposite sides that are not equal? (b) What does this tell you about the need to check R1 once R2 has been checked in a four-sided figure?
questions.a: (a) No. (b) Once all four angles are 90 degrees, the opposite sides turn out equal, so R1 will hold as well; a four-sided figure with R2 satisfied is a rectangle.
s: Part (a): No
Part (b): R2 forces R1, so R1 need not be tested separately

questions.q: True or False: A rectangle that is rotated so that its sides slant is no longer a rectangle, because its angles are no longer 90 degrees. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. Rotating changes neither the side lengths nor the angles, so all four angles are still 90 degrees and opposite sides are still equal; the rotated figure is still a rectangle.
s: States False
Correction: turning keeps lengths and angles, so R1 and R2 still hold

questions.q: Sunil says: 'A rotated square has the same sides and angles, so it is still a square. But a rotated rectangle may stop being a rectangle, because its sides tilt.' Is he right? Explain.
questions.a: Partly. The first part is right: the sides and angles of a rotated square do not change, so it is still a square. The second part is wrong: the same reasoning applies to a rectangle, whose opposite sides stay equal and angles stay 90 degrees, so a rotated rectangle is still a rectangle.
s: Verdict: partly right
Accepts the square part with the reason that lengths and angles are unchanged
Rejects the rectangle part by the same reasoning

questions.q: A designer sketches a figure with all angles 90 degrees and consecutive sides 5 cm, 5 cm, 7 cm and 7 cm. Show that no such figure exists.
questions.a: With all angles 90 degrees the figure is a rectangle, so opposite sides must be equal (R1). The sides 1st and 3rd are 5 cm and 7 cm, and the 2nd and 4th are 5 cm and 7 cm, so opposite sides are unequal. R1 fails, so a figure with these sides and four right angles cannot exist.
s: Uses all angles 90 degrees to say the figure is a rectangle
Identifies the opposite pairs as 5 and 7, which are unequal
Concludes that R1 fails, so the figure is impossible

questions.q: Write the side lengths of a four-sided figure that is a rectangle but not a square, and the side lengths of one that is a square. Then state in a line why the rectangle you wrote cannot be called a square.
questions.a: Rectangle: sides 9 cm, 4 cm, 9 cm, 4 cm with four right angles. Square: sides 6 cm, 6 cm, 6 cm, 6 cm with four right angles. The rectangle has unequal adjacent sides, so S1 fails and it is not a square. (Any valid values are accepted.)
s: A rectangle with opposite sides equal and adjacent sides unequal
A square with four equal sides
Says S1 fails for the rectangle

questions.q: Rectangle ABCD has its corners in that order around it. (a) How many valid names does it have in all, and why (think of where you may start and which way you may go)? (b) List the valid names that begin with C. (c) Of the 24 orders of the letters A, B, C, D, how many are not valid names? (d) Give two orders that are not valid. (e) Does a rotated copy of the rectangle have more valid names?
questions.a: (a) 8: any of the 4 corners may be the start and travel may go either way, 4 x 2 = 8. (b) CDAB and CBAD. (c) 24 - 8 = 16. (d) For example ABDC and ACBD. (e) No; rotating does not change the order of corners around the figure, so the 8 names are the same.
s: Part (a): 8, with 4 starting corners x 2 directions
Part (b): CDAB and CBAD
Part (c): 16
Part (d): two invalid orders such as ABDC and ACBD
Part (e): No, the order of corners is unchanged by rotation

questions.q: A carpenter measures four boards. Board 1: sides 90 cm, 60 cm, 90 cm, 60 cm, all angles 90 degrees. Board 2: sides 70 cm, 70 cm, 70 cm, 70 cm, all angles 90 degrees. Board 3: sides 90 cm, 60 cm, 90 cm, 60 cm, with angles 80, 100, 80 and 100 degrees. Board 4: sides 90 cm, 60 cm, 90 cm, 40 cm, all angles 90 degrees as measured. (a) Name the shape of Board 1. (b) Name the shape of Board 2, and say whether it also passes the rectangle test. (c) Why is Board 3 not a rectangle? (d) What is wrong with the measurements of Board 4? (e) Which boards pass the rectangle test as recorded?
questions.a: (a) A rectangle that is not a square: R1 and R2 hold, S1 does not. (b) A square; it also passes the rectangle test because its opposite sides are equal and its angles are 90 degrees. (c) R1 holds but R2 fails, since its angles are not all 90 degrees. (d) With all angles 90 degrees the opposite sides must be equal, but 60 cm and 40 cm are not, so the sides were mis-measured. (e) Boards 1 and 2 pass; Board 3 fails R2 and Board 4 fails R1 as recorded.
s: Part (a): rectangle, not a square
Part (b): square, and it also satisfies R1 and R2
Part (c): angles are not all 90 degrees, so R2 fails
Part (d): 60 cm and 40 cm opposite sides are unequal while angles are all 90 degrees, so R1 is violated
Part (e): Boards 1 and 2 pass, Boards 3 and 4 do not

questions.q: A workshop makes square cut-outs. An inspector has 40 minutes for a batch of 5 cut-outs and each measurement of a side or an angle takes 1 minute. She must decide for each cut-out whether it is a square. Plan P measures all 4 sides and all 4 angles. Plan Q measures all 4 angles and only 2 adjacent sides. Plan R measures only the 4 angles. (a) How many minutes does each plan need for the batch? Which fit within 40 minutes? (b) Explain from the chapter why the opposite sides need not be measured once all four angles are found to be 90 degrees. (c) What can Plan R establish about a cut-out, and what can it not? (d) Recommend a plan and justify it.
questions.a: (a) P: 8 x 5 = 40 min; Q: 6 x 5 = 30 min; R: 4 x 5 = 20 min. All three fit in 40 minutes. (b) A four-sided figure with all angles 90 degrees cannot have unequal opposite sides, so R1 follows from R2. (c) R shows the cut-out is a rectangle but cannot tell whether it is a square; a 4 cm by 6 cm rectangle passes. (d) P and Q both decide squareness. Q finishes in 30 minutes and uses the chapter's result that a rectangle with two adjacent sides equal is a square; P uses the whole 40 minutes and repeats checks that the angles already guarantee, though it would catch a slip in reading the ruler. Choose Q (10 minutes saved) unless readings are error-prone; R is ruled out because it cannot decide.
s: Part (a): 40, 30 and 20 minutes, with all three fitting
Part (b): all angles 90 degrees force opposite sides equal
Part (c): R proves a rectangle only, not a square, with an example
Part (d): P and Q both decide; chooses with the 10 minutes saved against the extra check, rejecting R

questions.q: A sign painter owns a square stencil of side 20 cm and a rectangular stencil of 30 cm by 20 cm. Job 1 is a square of side 20 cm painted tilted like a diamond. Job 2 is a rectangle 20 cm by 30 cm with the 30 cm sides vertical. Job 3 is a square of side 25 cm. For Job 3 he can buy a new square stencil for Rs 250, or rule each such square by hand at Rs 90 per square plus checking time. Checking all 4 sides and 4 angles takes 8 measurements; checking 4 angles and 2 adjacent sides takes 6; each measurement takes 1 minute and his time is worth Rs 5 per minute. (a) Can he use his own stencils for Jobs 1 and 2? Give the property that makes turning unimportant. (b) Which check of a hand-ruled 25 cm square is enough to show it is a square, and why? (c) Find the cost of one hand-ruled square with each check. (d) He expects exactly 2 such squares. Which method should he choose with each check? What if he expects 5?
questions.a: (a) Yes. Turning a stencil changes neither its sides nor its angles, so the same stencils give the tilted square and the upright rectangle. (b) The 6-measurement check is enough: four angles of 90 degrees make a rectangle, and two adjacent sides of 25 cm make it a square. (c) Full check: 90 + 8 x 5 = Rs 130; short check: 90 + 6 x 5 = Rs 120. (d) For 2 squares: full check costs Rs 260, more than Rs 250, so buy the stencil; short check costs Rs 240, so rule by hand. The choice therefore depends on whether the extra checks are needed. For 5 squares: Rs 650 or Rs 600 against Rs 250, so buy the stencil (saving Rs 350 or Rs 400).
s: Part (a): yes, because turning keeps lengths and angles
Part (b): 4 angles and 2 adjacent sides, with the reason
Part (c): Rs 130 and Rs 120
Part (d): 2 squares depends on the check (Rs 260 or Rs 240 against 250); 5 squares buy the stencil

questions.q: Hasan builds a square of side 9 cm by drawing PQ = 9 cm, a perpendicular at P with S marked 9 cm from P, and a perpendicular at Q with R marked 9 cm from Q. He then joins R and S. Without measuring, what can he say about RS and the angles at R and S?
questions.a: RS is 9 cm and both angles are 90 degrees, because the sides and angles already fixed make the figure a square
o: RS is 9 cm and both angles are 90 degrees, because the sides and angles already fixed make the figure a square
RS is 9 cm but the angles at R and S have to be measured, since only P and Q were drawn at 90 degrees
RS cannot be known, because a fourth side is free to take any length
The angles are 90 degrees but RS has to be measured, since the compass fixed only three sides

questions.q: Divya claims to have drawn a four-sided figure PQRS with all four angles measured as 90 degrees and with sides PQ = 6 cm, QR = 4 cm, RS = 5 cm and SP = 4 cm. Which comment is correct?
questions.a: Some measurement must be wrong, since a figure with four right angles has opposite sides equal and PQ and RS differ
o: Some measurement must be wrong, since a figure with four right angles has opposite sides equal and PQ and RS differ
The figure is correct, since it is a rectangle with two sides equal
The figure is correct, since four right angles do not make opposite sides equal
The angles must be wrong, since a rectangle needs sides 6, 5, 6, 5

questions.q: To construct a rectangle of sides 4 cm and 6 cm, Meena draws PQ = 6 cm as the base and then erects perpendiculars at P and Q. Which pair of distances should she mark on these two perpendiculars from P and Q?
questions.a: 4 cm from P and 4 cm from Q
o: 4 cm from P and 4 cm from Q
6 cm from P and 4 cm from Q
4 cm from P and 6 cm from Q
6 cm from P and 6 cm from Q

questions.q: A teacher draws worksheet squares by this routine: draw the base, a perpendicular at each end, mark the other two corners, join them. Each step takes 1 minute, except that marking a corner with a compass takes 0.4 minute; with a ruler it takes 1 minute. Opening and setting the compass to a new length takes 1 extra minute each time. Worksheet A needs 4 squares of different sides (3, 4, 5 and 6 cm); worksheet B needs 4 squares all of side 6 cm. (a) A square has 6 steps: base, perpendicular at P, marking S, perpendicular at Q, marking R, joining RS. How long does one square take with the ruler for marking, and why does she not need a seventh step of measuring RS and the angles at R and S? (b) How long does worksheet A take with the compass for marking? (c) How long does worksheet B take with the compass, setting it once? (d) Which method would you choose for each worksheet? questions.a: (a) 6 steps x 1 minute = 6 minutes. No seventh step is needed because with the perpendiculars at P and Q and PS = QR = 6 cm, the figure is a rectangle with all sides equal, so RS = 6 cm and the angles at R and S are 90 degrees automatically. (b) Each square: set the compass 1 + base 1 + perpendicular 1 + S 0.4 + perpendicular 1 + R 0.4 + join 1 = 5.8 minutes; 4 squares = 23.2 minutes (against 24 with the ruler). (c) 1 minute to set it once + 4 x 4.8 = 19.2 gives 20.2 minutes. (d) Worksheet B: compass, which saves 3.8 minutes and copies the same length each time. Worksheet A: the compass saves only 0.8 minute, so choose by accuracy against ease: the compass copies PQ without reading a ruler, while the ruler is easier if the compass legs slip.

Part (b): 23.2 minutes
Part (c): 20.2 minutes
Part (d): compass for B on time; A decided by the small saving of 0.8 minute against accuracy or ease

questions.q: A rectangle is constructed so that a diagonal splits a corner into 45 degrees and 45 degrees. (a) What shape is it? (b) One of its sides is 6 cm. What can you say about the other sides?
questions.a: (a) A square. (b) All the sides are 6 cm, because a diagonal splits a right angle into equal parts only when the rectangle is a square.
s: Part (a): a square
Part (b): all sides are 6 cm

questions.q: Two students each construct a rectangle in which a diagonal splits a corner into 50 degrees and 40 degrees. One draws the first side as 4 cm and the other as 7 cm. Can both be right? What does the angle split fix, and what does it leave open?
questions.a: Yes, both can be right. The angle split fixes the shape (how long the rectangle is compared with its width) but leaves the size open, so the first side may be drawn with any length.
s: Says both can be right
The split fixes the shape and leaves the size open (arbitrary first side)

questions.q: In the rectangle with a 60 degree and 30 degree split, the corner D can be located in two ways: by drawing a perpendicular at C, or by marking AD equal to BC with the compass. Which property of a rectangle does each way use?
questions.a: The perpendicular at C uses the property that all angles are 90 degrees (R2). Marking AD = BC uses the property that opposite sides are equal (R1).
s: Perpendicular at C uses R2, all angles 90 degrees
AD = BC uses R1, opposite sides equal

questions.q: True or False: In every rectangle, a diagonal divides each right angle at its two ends into two equal parts of 45 degrees. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. The two parts add up to 90 degrees but are equal only when the rectangle is a square. In a rectangle with unequal sides, such as one whose parts are 60 degrees and 30 degrees, they differ.
s: States False
Correction: the parts are equal (45 degrees each) only in a square

questions.q: Leela says: 'To locate B in the rectangle with side 5 cm and diagonal 7 cm, I must draw the full circle of radius 7 cm about D, and B is on that circle because it is 7 cm from D.' Is she right?
questions.a: Partly. B is on the circle, since B is 7 cm from D. But the full circle is not needed: only the arc near the perpendicular from C, where it will meet the line, has to be drawn.
s: Verdict: partly right
Accepts that B lies on the circle of radius 7 cm about D
Rejects the need for the full circle, since an arc near the line is enough

questions.q: Kabir says he can construct a rectangle with a side of 5 cm and a diagonal of 4 cm. Use what the chapter found about the nearest and farthest distances between points on opposite sides to show this is impossible.
questions.a: In a rectangle the farthest distance between a point on one side and a point on the opposite side is a diagonal, and the nearest distance is the side itself. A side is one of the possible distances, so the diagonal, being the farthest, cannot be shorter than a side. A diagonal of 4 cm is shorter than a side of 5 cm, so such a rectangle cannot exist.
s: Recalls that the diagonal is the farthest distance across the rectangle
The side is also one of the distances, so the diagonal must be at least as long
Concludes 4 cm against 5 cm is impossible

questions.q: Describe the steps, with the numbers used, to construct a rectangle having one side of 4 cm and a diagonal of 8 cm.
questions.a: Draw the side DC = 4 cm. Draw a perpendicular to DC at C. With the compass opened to 8 cm and the tip at D, draw an arc that crosses the perpendicular; the crossing point is B. Draw perpendiculars to DC at D and to BC at B; they meet at A, completing the rectangle.
s: Side DC = 4 cm and the perpendicular at C
Arc of radius 8 cm from D crossing the perpendicular at B
Perpendiculars at D and B meet at A

questions.q: A diagonal splits one right angle of four rectangles into these parts: R1: 60 degrees and an unknown part; R2: 45 degrees and an unknown part; R3: 33 degrees and an unknown part; R4: 50 degrees and an unknown part. (a) Find the unknown part in each. (b) Which rectangle is a square? (c) What does this tell you about its sides? (d) A fifth student reports parts of 47 degrees and 47 degrees. Can this be right? Why?
questions.a: (a) 30, 45, 57 and 40 degrees. (b) R2. (c) All its sides are equal. (d) No: the two parts of a right angle must add up to 90 degrees, and 47 + 47 = 94 degrees.
s: Part (a): 30, 45, 57 and 40 degrees
Part (b): R2
Part (c): all sides equal
Part (d): No, since 94 degrees is not 90

questions.q: Meera constructs a rectangle with a side DC = 3 cm and a diagonal of 7 cm. (a) State the first two steps. (b) State the centre and radius of the arc for B. (c) State how the fourth corner A is found. (d) Which properties, R1 and R2, should she check after drawing it? (e) She measures the other side as 6.3 cm. Is it longer or shorter than the side 3 cm, and is the diagonal longer than both sides?
questions.a: (a) Draw DC = 3 cm, then a perpendicular to DC at C. (b) Centre D, radius 7 cm. (c) Draw perpendiculars to DC at D and to BC at B; they meet at A. (d) R1: opposite sides equal, and R2: all angles 90 degrees. (e) 6.3 cm is longer than 3 cm, and the diagonal of 7 cm is longer than both sides.
s: Part (a): DC = 3 cm and the perpendicular at C
Part (b): centre D and radius 7 cm
Part (c): perpendiculars at D and B meet at A
Part (d): R1 and R2 stated

questions.q: A carpenter fits a diagonal brace in four rectangular frames ordered as squares for a school stage. At one corner of each frame the brace splits the right angle into two parts, measured with a protractor: F1 45 and 45 degrees; F2 38 and 52 degrees; F3 44 and 46 degrees; F4 50 and 40 degrees. The sides measured later are: F1 60 cm and 60 cm; F2 60 cm and 77 cm; F3 60 cm and 62 cm; F4 60 cm and 72 cm. Remaking a frame costs Rs 900. The committee says it will accept a 'square' whose sides differ by at most 2 cm, if that saves money. (a) Check that each pair of parts is consistent with a right angle. (b) By the chapter's rule on the angle split, which frames are exactly squares? (c) How do the side measurements agree with the angle readings for F3? (d) Which frames should be remade? Recommend, and give the cost.
questions.a: (a) 45 + 45 = 90, 38 + 52 = 90, 44 + 46 = 90 and 50 + 40 = 90, so all readings are consistent. (b) Only F1, since only there are the parts equal (45 and 45). (c) F3's parts are unequal, and its sides are also unequal (60 and 62), as a diagonal splits the angle equally only in a square. (d) F2 (sides 17 cm apart) and F4 (12 cm apart) must be remade, which costs 2 x 900 = Rs 1,800. F3 is not exactly a square but its sides differ by only 2 cm, which the committee accepts, saving Rs 900; if exact squares matter more than the saving, F3 can be remade too, bringing the cost to Rs 2,700.
s: Part (a): all four pairs add up to 90 degrees
Part (b): only F1
Part (c): unequal parts and unequal sides agree for F3
Part (d): remake F2 and F4 for Rs 1,800; accept F3 within 2 cm, with the alternative of Rs 900 more

questions.q: A notice is to be pasted in a gap on a board that is 6.5 cm long and 4.5 cm tall on the plan. The notice is drawn as a rectangle with a diagonal of exactly 7 cm, by the method of fixing a side and swinging an arc of 7 cm. Three versions are considered. Version A has a side of 5 cm and its other side then measures 4.9 cm. Version B has a side of 4 cm and its other side then measures 5.7 cm. Version C has a side of 3 cm and its other side then measures 6.3 cm. Each version can be placed with either side along the length of the gap. (a) Which versions fit the gap? (b) With each fitting version placed with its longer side along the length of the gap, state the spare length and the spare height it leaves. (c) For version A, what centre and radius of arc are used to mark the fourth point after the side is drawn and the perpendicular raised? (d) Recommend between the fitting versions, with reasons.
questions.a: (a) A does not fit: both its sides, 5 and 4.9 cm, exceed the gap height of 4.5 cm. B (5.7 by 4) and C (6.3 by 3) fit. (b) B leaves 6.5 - 5.7 = 0.8 cm of length and 4.5 - 4 = 0.5 cm of height; C leaves 6.5 - 6.3 = 0.2 cm of length and 4.5 - 3 = 1.5 cm of height. (c) Centre D (the end of the side DC away from the perpendicular at C) and radius 7 cm. (d) B leaves an even margin of 0.8 cm and 0.5 cm and is roomier for pasting; C is nearly the full length with only 0.2 cm to spare, so any small error will not fit but it leaves more height. Either is defensible: B for a safer margin in both directions, C if spare height matters more than spare length.
s: Part (a): A fails, B and C fit
Part (b): B leaves 0.8 and 0.5 cm; C leaves 0.2 and 1.5 cm
Part (c): centre D and radius 7 cm
Part (d): recommends B or C and weighs the 0.2 cm tightness of C against the 1.5 cm spare height

questions.q: Points B and C are marked. Ravi draws an arc of radius 6 cm centred at B and an arc of radius 4 cm centred at C, and they cross at P. He says, 'P is the same distance from B and C.' Which reply is correct?
questions.a: No; P is 6 cm from B and 4 cm from C, so equal radii would be needed for equal distances
o: No; P is 6 cm from B and 4 cm from C, so equal radii would be needed for equal distances
Yes; any crossing point of two arcs is equally far from both centres
Yes; P lies on both arcs, so it is 5 cm from each centre
No; P is 4 cm from B and 6 cm from C, because the smaller arc is nearer

questions.q: A class builds a bigger house in which every border line is 7 cm instead of 5 cm. What radius is set on the compass to find the roof point A from the two base corners, and to draw the curve from A through those corners?
questions.a: 7 cm for the arcs from both corners and 7 cm for the curve from A
o: 7 cm for the arcs from both corners and 7 cm for the curve from A
5 cm for the arcs and 7 cm for the curve from A
7 cm for the arcs and 14 cm for the curve from A
3.5 cm for the arcs and 7 cm for the curve from A

questions.q: In the House, A is found as the point 5 cm from both B and C. The arc drawn with the compass tip at A and radius 5 cm then passes through both B and C. What is the reason?
questions.a: Both B and C are 5 cm from A, which is the opening of the compass
o: Both B and C are 5 cm from A, which is the opening of the compass
A lies on the straight line joining B and C, so the arc has to touch both
B and C are the ends of the compass opening at the start
The arc is drawn after the straight lines, so it follows the lines AB and AC

questions.q: On a plan drawn so that 1 cm stands for 2 m, a fountain must be 9 m from lamp post L and 9 m from tree T. With the compass tip at L and then at T, what radius is set to draw the arcs?
questions.a: 4.5 cm
o: 4.5 cm
9 cm
18 cm

questions.q: Mina plans three drawings: (i) a circle of radius 3 cm around a marked dot, (ii) a face whose two eye curves are centred at points that are not marked on the paper but must lie at the same level, (iii) a square built from a given base. For which drawing does she need a supporting line, and what does she do with it?
questions.a: Drawing (ii): she draws a faint horizontal line to place both compass centres at the same level, then rubs it out
o: Drawing (ii): she draws a faint horizontal line to place both compass centres at the same level, then rubs it out
Drawing (i): she draws a faint line through the dot, which must stay in the finished circle
Drawing (iii): she draws a faint curved line for the base, which stays as the bottom of the square
All three, because every construction needs a faint line that stays in the figure

questions.q:
To find a point that is 5 cm from point B and also 5 cm from point C:
Statement 1: Arcs of radius 5 cm centred at B and at C are enough, without the full circles.
Statement 2: The point where the two arcs cross is 5 cm from B and 5 cm from C.
Statement 3: The same method with radius 7 cm gives a point 7 cm from both B and C.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: all three
o: all three
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): To find the roof point A of the House, only part of each circle, an arc, has to be drawn.
Reason (R): All the points of a circle are at the same distance from its centre.
questions.a: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: On a plan where 1 cm stands for 3 m, a tree is to be 12 m from each of two lamp posts. The radius of each arc on the plan is ___ cm.

Match each item in Column I with what it is in Column II.
Column I: 1. The crossing point of two 5 cm arcs centred at B and C  2. A faint line drawn only to help placing the compass  3. The arc drawn from A, 5 cm in radius, in the House  4. The circle of radius 7 cm centred at D in the rectangle with a 5 cm side and 7 cm diagonal
Column II: A. A curve passing through B and C  B. A point 5 cm from both B and C  C. The place that fixes the corner at the given diagonal length  D. A supporting figure not part of the final drawing

On a plan with 1 cm for 5 m, a well must be 40 m from each of two pillars P1 and P2. (a) What radius on the plan is used for the two arcs? (b) Why are two arcs, one centred at each pillar, needed rather than only one?
questions.a: (a) 40 / 5 = 8 cm. (b) One arc gives all the points 8 cm from one pillar only; the well must be 8 cm from both pillars, so it is the point where the two arcs cross.
s: Part (a): 8 cm
Part (b): the well must be at the right distance from both centres, which is the crossing point

questions.q: To find the roof point A, one student slides a ruler around until a point is 5 cm from B and from C, while another uses two arcs. Give two ways the arcs method is better.
questions.a: The arcs method needs no trial and error, since the crossing point is the answer. It also makes the distance to both B and C exactly the compass opening, so no point has to be checked by repeated measuring.
s: No trial and error
Distance from B and C fixed by the compass opening, so exact

questions.q: A bigger house has all its border lines 7 cm. (a) State the radius for the arcs from the two base corners and for the roof curve. (b) After A is found, which two lengths are checked to be 7 cm to confirm the roof curve will pass through both base corners?
questions.a: (a) 7 cm for the arcs and 7 cm for the roof curve. (b) The distances from A to each of the two base corners; both should be 7 cm.
s: Part (a): 7 cm for arcs and roof curve
Part (b): A to each base corner

questions.q: The corners B and C of a house base are 7 cm apart. Tara tries to find a point A that is 3 cm from both by drawing short arcs of radius 3 cm round B and round C. Will the arcs cross? Give the reason.
questions.a: No. A point 3 cm from B and 3 cm from C would give a path B to A to C of only 6 cm, which is shorter than the 7 cm between B and C, so the arcs of radius 3 cm can never meet; a larger radius, more than 3.5 cm, is needed.
s: States that the arcs will not cross
Reason: 3 + 3 = 6 is less than 7 (the radius must exceed half of BC)

questions.q: True or False: To find the point A that is 5 cm from both B and C, it is not necessary to draw two full circles; short arcs of radius 5 cm centred at B and C are enough. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. The point A lies where the arcs cross, so only the parts of the circles near that place are needed; the rest of each circle is never used.
s: States True
Reason: only the region where the arcs cross matters

questions.q: Nisha says: 'After finding A, the roof curve must be drawn with a compass opening different from 5 cm, because it is a new part of the figure.' Is she right?
questions.a: No. The curve is drawn with the tip at A, and B and C are each 5 cm from A, so the opening must stay 5 cm for the curve to pass through both B and C. A different opening would miss at least one of them.
s: Verdict: No
Uses that A is 5 cm from B and from C
Says another opening would miss B or C

questions.q: Rahul says: 'In the bigger house with all lines 7 cm, the arcs from the two base corners have radius 7 cm, and the base corners stay 5 cm apart.' Is he right?
questions.a: No. The base is one of the lines of the house, so its corners must now be 7 cm apart. The arcs of radius 7 cm are right, but a base of 5 cm would not make all lines 7 cm.
s: Verdict: No
The base corners must also be 7 cm apart
The arcs of radius 7 cm are correct, so only the base needs to change

questions.q: Describe a real situation in which a point must be a given distance from each of two fixed places, and show how to find that point on a plan using a scale you choose.
questions.a: For example, a drinking-water tap must be 30 m from the school gate and 30 m from the playground entrance. On a plan with 1 cm for 10 m the radius is 3 cm. Draw an arc of 3 cm centred at the gate and another centred at the entrance; the tap goes where they cross. (Any consistent situation is accepted.)
s: A realistic situation with two places and the same required distance
A scale and the radius worked out from it
Arcs centred at both places crossing at the required point

questions.q: On a plan drawn so that 1 cm stands for 4 m, a school wants a bench 12 m from the gate G and 12 m from the canteen K, and a second bench 16 m from both. (a) What radius is set for the first bench? (b) What is the radius for the second bench? (c) State where the first bench is placed once the arcs are drawn. (d) Which bench needs the larger compass opening? (e) What stays the same in the two constructions?
questions.a: (a) 12 / 4 = 3 cm. (b) 16 / 4 = 4 cm. (c) At the point where the two 3 cm arcs, centred at G and at K, cross. (d) The second bench, with 4 cm. (e) The method: one arc centred at each of the two places with the same radius, and the bench at the crossing.
s: Part (a): 3 cm
Part (b): 4 cm
Part (c): the crossing of the arcs centred at G and K
Part (d): second bench, 4 cm
Part (e): equal arcs from the two places, bench at the crossing

questions.q: A class draws six Houses on a chart, where every line of a House equals its compass opening: two Houses of 5 cm, two of 7 cm and two of 9 cm. For each House the same compass opening finds the roof point and draws the roof curve. Each time the compass opening has to be changed (and once at the start) it takes 1 minute. (a) Why does one opening serve a whole House? (b) How many settings are needed if the Houses are drawn in the order 5, 7, 9, 5, 7, 9? (c) How many if drawn in the order 5, 5, 7, 7, 9, 9? (d) How many minutes does the second order save? (e) Which order would you advise, and what must be remembered about the Houses drawn with the same opening?
questions.a: (a) A is found 5, 7 or 9 cm from both base corners using that radius, and the roof curve from A passes through the corners with the same radius, so no new opening is needed. (b) The size changes after every House, so 1 setting at the start plus 5 changes: 6 settings. (c) 3 settings. (d) 6 - 3 = 3 minutes. (e) The second order (same sizes together), since it needs fewer changes; the opening must not be disturbed between the two Houses of the same size.
s: Part (a): the arcs and the roof curve use the same radius
Part (b): 6 settings
Part (c): 3 settings
Part (d): 3 minutes
Part (e): advises grouping equal sizes and keeping the opening undisturbed

questions.q: On a plan drawn so that 1 cm stands for 4 m, a statue is to be placed at the same distance from two lamp posts, found as the crossing of two arcs. Electric cable of Rs 80 per metre must run from the statue to each lamp post. The safety rule says the statue must be at least 23 m from each post. The budget for cable is Rs 3,600. (a) Find the compass radius on the plan and the cable cost if the statue is 20 m from each post. (b) Find the same for 24 m. (c) Show that neither of these is a good choice, and say why. (d) Another possibility is 22 m. Recommend a distance, using the rule and the budget, and say what compromise your recommendation involves.
questions.a: (a) 20 / 4 = 5 cm; cable 2 x 20 x 80 = Rs 3,200. (b) 24 / 4 = 6 cm; cable 2 x 24 x 80 = Rs 3,840. (c) 20 m breaks the safety rule (it is less than 23 m); 24 m meets the rule but costs Rs 240 more than the Rs 3,600 budget. (d) 22 m costs 2 x 22 x 80 = Rs 3,520, within budget but 1 m short of the rule; 23 m costs Rs 3,680, which is Rs 80 over budget. The 22 m choice breaks the stated safety rule, so the recommendation is 23 m (5.75 cm radius) with a request for Rs 80 more; 22 m is acceptable only if the rule is formally relaxed.
s: Part (a): radius 5 cm and Rs 3,200
Part (b): radius 6 cm and Rs 3,840
Part (c): 20 m breaks the rule, 24 m exceeds the budget by Rs 240
Part (d): recommends 23 m with Rs 80 extra or 22 m, naming the compromise

questions.q: On a fair ground plan with 1 cm for 5 m, the two gates G1 and G2 are 6 cm apart. A food stall is to be placed by drawing arcs of equal radius from the two gates, 25 m from each gate; a first-aid post is to be 20 m from each gate in the same way. Power cable costs Rs 150 per metre, and each stall is supplied from both gates for safety. The fair committee has Rs 13,000 for cable. (a) What radius on the plan is used for each stall? (b) Find the cable cost for each stall. (c) Find the total and by how much it is above or below the budget. (d) The committee can either supply the first-aid post from one gate only, or ask for more money. Give your recommendation and what each choice costs or risks.
questions.a: (a) Food stall: 25 / 5 = 5 cm; first-aid post: 20 / 5 = 4 cm. (b) Food stall: 2 x 25 x 150 = Rs 7,500; first-aid post: 2 x 20 x 150 = Rs 6,000. (c) Total Rs 13,500, which is Rs 500 over the budget. (d) Supplying the first-aid post from one gate only costs 20 x 150 = Rs 3,000, bringing the total to Rs 10,500, but leaves the post without power if that line fails. Asking for Rs 500 more keeps both lines. A defensible recommendation is to ask for the extra Rs 500, since first aid is the last place to cut safety; the saving of Rs 3,000 would be reasonable only if the committee has a backup supply.
s: Part (a): 5 cm and 4 cm
Part (b): Rs 7,500 and Rs 6,000
Part (c): Rs 13,500, Rs 500 over
Part (d): recommends a choice, weighing Rs 500 extra against the Rs 3,000 saving and the loss of the second line
